steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper about a global prompt hacking competition we ran to find out how vulnerable LLMs are to prompt injection. It should explain why prompt-controlled LLM applications are a security concern, what existing work is missing, and what the competition and the resulting dataset contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs are everywhere
2. Prompts as the control interface, and the attack surface they open
3. Prompt hacking in an application-grounded setting
4. Gap in existing work -> competition, dataset, taxonomy

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs are everywhere
- InstructGPT, BLOOM, GPT-4; widely deployed in consumer-facing, interactive settings
- companies in diverse sectors: startups to well established corporations
- tasks from spell correction to military command and control

2. Prompts and the attack surface
- many applications controlled through prompts
- prompt = natural language string instructing the llm what to do
- flexibility -> accessible entry into powerful llm s
- but: rapidly expanding attack surface -> leak private information; offensive or biased content; mass-produced harmful/misleading messages
- umbrella term: prompt hacking = adversarial prompts to elicit malicious results

3. Application-grounded setting (Figure 1)
- llm instructed to do a downstream task (e.g. story generation)
- attackers try to make it produce a target malicious output (e.g. a key phrase)
- requires creativity to overrule the original instructions

4. Gap and contributions
- existing prompt injection work (Section 2): small-scale case studies, qualitative analysis
- limits understanding of how susceptible SOTA LLMs are + which attack types more likely to succeed (-> need more defenses)
- crowdsource adversarial prompts at massive scale via global prompt hacking competition; valuable prizes to motivate competitors, simulate real-world scenarios (Section 3)
- over 2800 participants, 600K+ adversarial prompts -> resource on systemic vulnerabilities of llm s like Chat gpt (Section 4)
- dataset on HuggingFace
- taxonomical ontology of the collected prompts (Section 5)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (llm s) like InstructGPT, BLOOM and GPT-4 are now deployed widely in settings that are consumer-facing and interactive. All kinds of companies, from startups to well established corporations, are using llm s, and the tasks go from spell correction all the way to military command and control.

A lot of these applications are controlled with prompts. Here, by a prompt we mean a natural language string that tells the llm what to do. This approach is flexible, and that gives people an accessible way into using powerful llm s. But it also means there is an attack surface that is expanding quickly, and it can be used to leak private information, to generate offensive or biased content, and to mass-produce messages that are harmful or misleading. In general we can call these attempts prompt hacking, which means using adversarial prompts to get malicious results.

- application-grounded setting (Figure 1): llm instructed to do a downstream task (e.g. story generation); attackers try to get a target malicious output (e.g. a key phrase); need creativity to overrule the original instructions
- existing prompt injection work (Section 2) only small-scale case studies / qualitative analysis -> limits understanding of how susceptible SOTA LLMs are and which attacks more likely to succeed (need more defenses)
- our fix: crowdsource adversarial prompts at massive scale via global prompt hacking competition, valuable prizes to motivate + simulate real-world scenarios (Section 3)
- over 2800 participants, 600K+ adversarial prompts; resource on systemic vulnerabilities of llm s like Chat gpt (Section 4); dataset on HuggingFace
- taxonomical ontology of the collected prompts (Section 5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (llm s) like InstructGPT, BLOOM and GPT-4 are now deployed widely in settings that are consumer-facing and interactive. All kinds of companies, from startups to well established corporations, are using llm s, and the tasks go from spell correction all the way to military command and control.

A lot of these applications are controlled with prompts. Here, by a prompt we mean a natural language string that tells the llm what to do. This approach is flexible, and that gives people an accessible way into using powerful llm s. But it also means there is an attack surface that is expanding quickly, and it can be used to leak private information, to generate offensive or biased content, and to mass-produce messages that are harmful or misleading. In general we can call these attempts prompt hacking, which means using adversarial prompts to get malicious results.

In this paper we focus on prompt hacking in a setting that is grounded in an application (Figure 1). The llm is instructed to do some downstream task (for example story generation), but the attackers try to manipulate it so that it generates a target malicious output (for example a key phrase). To overrule the original instructions, the attackers often have to be creative in how they design their prompts.

Existing work on prompt injection (Section 2) only does small-scale case studies or qualitative analysis. Because of this we do not understand well how susceptible state-of-the-art LLMs are to prompt injection, and we also do not have a systematic understanding of which types of attacks are more likely to succeed and therefore need more defense strategies. To fill this gap we crowdsource adversarial prompts at a massive scale with a global prompt hacking competition. The competition gives the winners valuable prizes, to motivate competitors and to closely simulate real-world prompt hacking scenarios (Section 3). Over 2800 participants took part and contributed 600K+ adversarial prompts, so we collect a valuable resource for analyzing the systemic vulnerabilities of llm s such as Chat gpt to malicious manipulation (Section 4). The dataset is available on HuggingFace. We also give a comprehensive taxonomical ontology of the adversarial prompts we collected (Section 5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (llm s) such as InstructGPT [1], BLOOM [2], and GPT-4 [3] are now widely deployed in consumer-facing and interactive settings [4]. Companies in diverse sectors, from startups to well established corporations, use llm s for tasks that range from spell correction to military command and control [5].

Many of these applications are controlled through prompts. In our context, a prompt is a natural language string that instructs the llm what to do [6,7,8,9]. The flexibility of this approach offers an accessible entry into using powerful llm s [10,11], but it also reveals a rapidly expanding attack surface that can leak private information [12], generate offensive or biased content [13], and mass-produce harmful or misleading messages [14]. These attempts can be generalized as prompt hacking: using adversarial prompts to elicit malicious results [15]. This paper focuses on prompt hacking in an application-grounded setting (Figure 1), where a llm is instructed to perform a downstream task (e.g., story generation) while attackers try to manipulate it into generating a target malicious output (e.g., a key phrase). Attackers often need to be creative when designing prompts that overrule the original instructions.

Existing work on prompt injection (Section 2) is limited to small-scale case studies or qualitative analysis. This limits our understanding of how susceptible state-of-the-art LLMs are to prompt injection, as well as our systematic understanding of which types of attacks are more likely to succeed and therefore need more defense strategies. To fill this gap, we crowdsource adversarial prompts at a massive scale through a global prompt hacking competition, which gives winners valuable prizes in order to motivate competitors and closely simulate real-world prompt hacking scenarios (Section 3). With over 2800 participants contributing 600K+ adversarial prompts, we collect a valuable resource for analyzing the systemic vulnerabilities of llm s such as Chat gpt to malicious manipulation (Section 4). This dataset is available on HuggingFace. We also provide a comprehensive taxonomical ontology for the collected adversarial prompts (Section 5).
